ROLEPLAYER CARD NO. 4

SETTING Community Health Centre

PATIENT You are 25. You have an outbreak of ulcers on your tongue which started last
night. You have suffered from these on and off since you were a child, including
several attacks in recent months. Usually they clear up after a few days. Six
months ago you started working as a salesperson. It is a high-pressure job. You
need to talk a lot and often entertain clients. The mouth ulcers really bother
you when speaking, eating or drinking. You feel irritable with them and you are
also worried that your work is being affected. You are generally well. |

TASK Answer the doctor's questions about your general health.

Ask for something to clear up your ulcers within 24 hours (you have to speak at
an important meeting tomorrow).

e Insist on something more effective than antiseptic gel from the pharmacy - it
never helps much.

Try to find out what causes the ulcers and how to stop them from recuming.

CANDIDATE CARD NO. 4 MEDICINE

SETTING Community Health Centre

DOCTOR The patient, aged 25, presents with tiny, off-white ulcers on the tongue. On
examination, the patient clearly has good dental hygiene.

TASK © Question the patient to exclude diabetes mellitus and inflammatory bowel
disease as underlying conditions, and herpes simplex as a cause (fever
symptoms?).

e You suspect aphthous ulcers (no known cause, but some research suggests an
immune reaction - could be related to stress, hormones, virus or allergy).
e Recommend a blood test to check for infection.
¢ Discuss management of the symptoms (rinse with warm, salty water or
| medicated mouthwash, apply antiseptic gel, take paracetamol, have plenty of
| fluids, avoid spicy and sour foods).
© The ulcers will resolve by themselves in a few days.
© Offer to prescribe an anti-inflammatory drug if pain persists.
| ¢ Advise the patient on a healthy lifestyle.

| © Cambridge Boxhill Language Assessment 7 MARCH 2014

SETTING Emergency Department

PATIENT You are a 26-year-old student who recently returned from an overseas vacation.
You have felt as though you have had flu symptoms for a couple of days, but have
not had a sore throat or cough. Your friend believes you may have malaria and has
convinced you to present to the Emergency Department (ED) to be assessed.

TASK e Answer the doctor's questions: you-have just been on a three-week trip to a
tropical area and returned three days ago; you were bitten by many mosauitos.

¢ Tell the doctor that you have had some flu-like symptoms (slight temperature,
headaches, joint aches but no rash) for a few days and always feel worse by the
end of the day.

e Express concern that you will have to spend more time in the ED.Explain that
you have several work and study commitments and don't have time to be sick.

* Reluctantly agree to stay in the ED and have some blood tests to exclude other |
diseases, and agree to outpatient follow-up with a general practitioner (GP). |

SETTING Emergency Department

DOCTOR Your patient is a 26-year-old student who returned from an overseas vacation
recently. The patient has felt as though he/she has had flu symptoms for a couple
of days, but has not had a sore throat or cough. His/her friend has convinced the
student to present to the Emergency Department (ED) to be assessed for malaria.

TASK ¢ Ask the patient about travel in the past two weeks, and ask about mosquito

exposure.

© Find out about the symptoms (e.g., temperature, headaches, joint aches, rash,
etc.).

¢ Discuss possible diagnoses (e.g., malaria, dengue fever, etc.) but explain that it |
is probably a non-specific viral disease.

e Reassure the patient that there is no need for admission to the ED but suggest
some basic blood tests in the ED and follow-up with the patient’s general
practitioner (GP).

e Persuade the patient to stay in the ED now for blood tests.

Emergency Department

You are 50 years old and were lifting weights at the gymnasium this morning when
you dropped a 20kg weight on your left foot. You have come to the Emergonoy
Department to have your foot treated and to get a cast put on it as you are sure
you have broken it. You are experiencing a lot of pain.

* Explain that you lift weights every day but today you became distracted and
dropped a weight on your foot.

Stress that your whole foot hurts — not just your little toe — and demand that a
cast be fitted.

* Become frustrated and insist that rest and elevation is not enough to heal your
foot - you believe that a cast will support its rehabilitation.

* Ask what can be done for your foot if a cast is not appropriate.

* Eventually accept the doctor's suggestion of a splint and ask what you can do
about the pain.

OET AUGUST 2015

Emergency Department

You are speaking to a 50-year-old who dropped a 20kg weight on his/her left foot
this morning when he/she was lifting weights at the gymnasium. He/she has come
to the Emergency Department to have the foot treated and to get a cast as he/she
thinks it is broken. On examination you confirm that only the little toe is broken.

« Explain that the little toe is broken but should heal by itself with proper care
(e.g., elevation, ice, rest, avoid putting weight on it, etc.),

* Explain that a cast will not help the toe to heal and will cause difficulties with
mobility.

* Stress that fitting a cast will cause atrophy of other muscles in the leg making
rehabilitation more difficult.

« Persuade the patient that a splint on the toe would be more beneficial than a
cast,

* Recommend paracetamol! for pain relief and wearing sturdy shoes until the toe
heals (in about 6 weeks).

Emergency Department of a Large Metropolitan Hospital

You are the parent of a four-year-old boy who presented two hours agoto the ~~
Emergency Department (ED) with a 36-hour history of recurrent vomiting and
stomach pain. Tho boy's vomit consisted of mainly clear slightly bile-stained fluid,
with no sign of blood. He felt thirsty and wanted to drink water but was not able to
keep any down, The doctor told you that your son had viral gastroenteritis. He was
kept in for two hours on oral re-hydration fluids and now the doctor tells you that it
is safe for him-to return home. You are anxious and confused about his condition.

© Seek'an explanation of viral gastroenteritis (‘How did my son get this? Is it
infectious?’). i

* Your son looks very weak. Demand that the doctor hospitalise him for expert
care.

* You are worried about supporting your son's recovery at home. Seek
reassurance that he will improve if he returns home. Ask ‘Will my son be safe?’

EC ANDIDATE CARD NO.2

MEDICINE

Emergency Department of a Large Metropolitan Hospital

A parent presented two hours ago at the Emergency Department (ED) with his/her
four-year-old son. The boy has a 36-hour history of recurrent vomiting and
stomach pain. On presentation, the boy's vomit consisted of clear slightly
bile-stained fluid, with no blood. He felt thirsty but was unable to keep anything
down, You suspect viral gastroenteritis. He was given oral re-hydration fluids and
observed for two hours and now you tell the parent that it is safe to discharge him.
The parent becomes anxious..:

* Respond to the parent's questions. Explain viral gastroenteritis (e.g., an irritation
of stomach or intestines due to infection with a virus, etc.).

* Explain that oral re-hydration therapy is usually effective without the need for
hospitalisation.

* Convince the parent that it is safe to take his/her son home but to seek medical
advice if he shows signs of severe dehydration (e.g., rapid heartbeat and
breathing, weak pulse, etc.).
